<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely tight, well-focused debate that correctly narrowed to one clause: whether a non-monitored option must be priced without a selection load. A's reframe was excellent — telematics as the first tool that lets conduct override zip code, credit score and demographics, with the motion's cap recast as a "subsidy from the transparent to the opaque." That line stayed live to the end. But B blunted A's decisive-looking attack. B showed "ordinary actuarial factors" already include the driver's own crashes, tickets and mileage, collapsing A's zip-code-versus-telematics dichotomy; B named the payer honestly under pressure (monitored drivers via a capped discount) and analogised it to the cost every insurer absorbs for classifications it declines to use, which downgraded A's "arithmetically impossible" charge to a mere fairness complaint. B's dilemma was the sharpest move of the round: a capped discount still attracts safe drivers if the signal is strong, so if the discount must be big enough to make refusal unaffordable, CON has conceded coercion. A answered the coercion-line question directly and well (gap equals real loss difference; excessive-rate regulation), but in doing so conceded there is no ceiling and that the gap grows automatically with adoption — which B crystallised into the cleanest decision rule on the table: in a market the state compels you to enter, may the price of refusing surveillance rise without limit? A's credit-check and crash-test analogies were answered squarely (you can live without credit; you cannot lawfully drive uninsured). A also carries slightly less clipping cost, and B's "ordinary cost of doing business" shrug was its weakest moment, so the margin is narrow rather than comfortable.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to the "who pays?" pressure question: naming monitored drivers through a capped discount, then converting it into a dilemma — if a capped discount cannot attract safe drivers, the business model depends on making refusal unaffordable, which concedes coercion. This defanged A's central "arithmetically impossible" attack and set up B's closing frame about an unlimited, self-escalating price on refusal.</best_rebuttal>
